title: Butter lamps
hookLine: lamps of butter offered in temples as light

cards: The smell reaches you before the light does: warm, a little smoky, a little like a kitchen. Then the room opens up.
Row after row of small metal bowls on long shelves, each holding a soft pool of melted butter and a single cotton wick, each burning.
A woman in a long apron walks the rows with a pitcher, topping them up, the way someone waters plants.
A pilgrim beside her tips a spoonful of butter from a jar she carried from home into one bowl, and moves on without a word. In Tibetan temples, light is something you give.

teach.h: A BOWL OF BUTTER AND A WICK.
teach.b: First, what it is. A butter lamp is a bowl of clarified butter with a wick, set before an image of the Buddha on a home shrine or in a temple hall. Tibetans call it chöme, an offering lamp.
Families light them at home; pilgrims bring butter, or pay a little for a lamp to be lit, and temples keep many burning through the day.
Light sits among the classic shrine offerings, with water, flowers, incense and food. Second, what the light means.
Tibetan teachers explain the lamp as wisdom, the light that clears away the darkness of not seeing. Lighting one wishes that clarity for yourself and for others.
People light them on holy days, for someone who is sick, and for someone who has died, the flame carrying a wish the way a letter carries words.
Third, a story you met back in year one: the poor woman's lamp. She had almost nothing, begged a few coins, bought a little oil, and lit one small lamp among the grand lamps of kings.
By morning the great lamps had burned out. Hers still burned, and when a disciple tried to put it out, it would not go out.
In the story, the Buddha says it burns on because of the heart that lit it.
Fourth, so the offering isn't measured by how much butter is in the bowl. A spoonful from a jar carried from home counts.
The tradition cares about the intention: the wish that someone, somewhere, sees a little more clearly because of it.

how: Tibetan Buddhists light butter lamps on home shrines and in temples, often bringing butter as an offering, and light them on holy days, for the sick and for the dead; the flame is explained as wisdom dispelling darkness.

o: bowls of butter with a wick, lit before the Buddha
lanterns floated on a river to honor the dead
candles lit in a temple to keep away spirits

s: a butter lamp only counts if it is large and costly
in the story of the poor woman, her one small lamp outlasts the lamps of kings.
Tibetan teachers explain the lamp's light as wisdom
the light clearing darkness stands for wisdom clearing away not seeing.
people light lamps for the sick and for those who have died

games.q: you're the poor woman. you have a few coins, and the kings have lit grand lamps. what do you do?
o: stay home: your gift is too small to matter.
buy a little oil and light one small lamp.
wait until you can afford a lamp as grand as theirs.
games.why: she lights one small lamp. in the story, by morning it is the one still burning, because of the heart that lit it.

practice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it; if not, a small lamp or even a phone screen turned low will do.
Watch the flame for a few breaths, and let it stand for a wish: that someone you know sees their way a little more clearly today. When you're done, blow it out gently.

wordCard.voice: Butter lamps. Small bowls of butter and a wick, lit before the Buddha in Tibetan homes and temples: light offered as a sign of wisdom clearing the dark. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali dipa, a lamp; Tibetans call the offering lamp chöme.

carryVoice: Your line: a lamp offered. A spoonful from home counts, lit with the whole heart. Go gently.
